# Dīghanakha Sutta (MN 74 (PTS MN i 497))

**ID:** MN 74 (PTS MN i 497)  
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Dīghanakha Sutta  
**Title (English, from literature):** With Dīghanakha  
**PTS:** MN i 497  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul2.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul2.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dīghanakha Sutta* is the 74th discourse of the *Majjhima Nikāya* (PTS MN i 497). In this discourse, the wanderer (or renouncer) Dīghanakha approaches the Buddha and asserts the skeptical view that "nothing is acceptable to me" (*sabbam me na khamati*) [Anderson 1999]. In response, the Buddha critiques this position alongside its alternatives ("everything is acceptable to me" and "some things are acceptable and some are not"), demonstrating how extreme skepticism and the grasping of views lead to disputation [Anderson 1999; Emmanuel 2013]. Rather than becoming trapped in conceptual abstractions, the Buddha redirects attention to living experience by examining the physical body and the three types of feeling (pleasant, painful, and neutral), which arise in dependence on contact and are mutually exclusive [Anālayo 2014; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The discourse famously concludes with Sāriputta—standing nearby and reflecting on the Buddha's instruction to abandon and let go through direct insight—attaining full liberation (arahantship), while Dīghanakha attains the "dhamma-eye" (stream-entry) [Anālayo 2010; Anderson 1999; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The text also emphasizes that a liberated adept uses conventional speech without grasping or adhering to it [Powers 2016; Emmanuel 2013].

In addition, early Sanskrit Buddhist literature such as the *Mahāvastu* preserves ancient recensions of the discourse [Lamotte 1988; Nariman 1919].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: Avs 99 Dīrghanakhaḥ; SA2 203 長爪; SA 969 長爪; T 1509.1a 大智度論; T 1545.98 阿毘達磨大毘婆沙論 1; T 200.90 長爪梵志緣; Xct Mu Kd Eimer རབ་ཏུ་འབྱུང་བའི་གཞི (Pravrajyā-vastu)
- Resembling parallels: SF 133; SF 81 Dīrghanakha
- Mentioned in: Mnd 11 Kalahavivādasuttaniddesa; Mnd 12 Cūḷabyūhasuttaniddesa

**Sources**

- [Powers 2016] John Powers, ed., The Buddhist World (2016) — Discussion of the sutta's view on liberated monks using conventional speech without adhering to it.
- [Emmanuel 2013] Steven M. Emmanuel, ed., A Companion to Buddhist Philosophy (2013) — Note on the adept agreeing and disputing with no one and using conventions without erring.
- [Anālayo 2010] Bhikkhu Anālayo, From Grasping to Emptiness: Excursions into the Thought-world of the Pali Discourses (2010) — Observation on Sāriputta's awakening upon hearing the instruction on giving up views through insight.
- [Lamotte 1988] Étienne Lamotte, History of Indian Buddhism (1988 [1958]) — Citation of Dīghanakhasutta in the Mahāvastu.
- [Nariman 1919] G. K. Nariman, Literary History of Sanskrit Buddhism (1919) — Note on the presence of the Dīghanakhasutta in the Mahāvastu.
- [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Summary of content (sceptic, contemplation of feelings, Sāriputta's arahantship) and body contemplation.
- [Anderson 1999] Carol S. Anderson, Pain and its Ending: The Four Noble Truths in the Theravāda Buddhist Canon (1999) — Detailed analysis of Dīghanakha's view 'sabbam me na khamati', the Buddha's response, and the spiritual attainments of Dīghanakha and Sāriputta.
- [Anālayo 2014] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Perspectives on Satipaṭṭhāna (2014) — Detailed examination of the contemplation of feelings, its role in Sāriputta's awakening, and parallels in Saṃyuktāgama, Avadānaśataka, and Vinayavastu.
